interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: ViDR: Grounding Multimodal Deep Research Reports in Source Visual Evidence
papers.authors: Zhuofan Shi , Peilun Jia , Baoqin Sun , Haiyang Shen , Sixiong Xie , Yun Ma , Xiang Jing
papers.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Information Retrieval (cs.IR)
papers.abstract: Recent deep research systems have improved the ability of large language models to produce long, grounded reports through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, most text-centered systems rely mainly on textual evidence, while multimodal systems often retrieve images only weakly or generate charts themselves, leaving source figures underused as evidence. We present ViDR, a multimodal deep research framework that grounds long-form reports in source figures. ViDR treats source figures as retrievable, interpretable, routable, and verifiable evidence objects, while still generating analytical charts when needed. It builds an evidence-indexed outline linking claims to textual and visual evidence, refines noisy web images into source-figure evidence atoms through context-aware filtering, outline-aware reranking, and VLM-based visual analysis, and generates each section with section-specific evidence. ViDR further validates visual references to reduce hallucinated or misplaced figures. We also introduce MMR Bench+, a benchmark for evaluating visual evidence use in deep research reports, covering source-figure retrieval, placement, interpretation, verifiability, and analytical chart generation. Experiments show that ViDR improves overall report quality, source-figure integration, and verifiability over strong commercial and open-source baselines. These results suggest that source visual evidence is important for multimodal deep research, as it strengthens evidential grounding, visual support, and report verifiability.
papers.Reasons for match: Multimodal deep research framework grounding reports in source figures; directly applicable to astronomical literature review and data analysis.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how to generate long-form research reports that properly cite and use source figures, not just text. It presents ViDR, a framework that treats source figures as retrievable, interpretable, and verifiable evidence, building an evidence-indexed outline and refining noisy web images into structured evidence atoms. This is highly relevant for astronomy because astronomers often need to synthesize results from papers with figures (e.g., spectra, images, SEDs). An astronomer could use ViDR to automatically generate literature reviews that include relevant figures from JWST papers, with proper attribution. The framework also validates visual references to reduce hallucinations. A limitation is that it requires a large corpus of web images and may need adaptation for specialized astronomical figure formats (e.g., FITS files).
Full-text inspection checklist: Check how the framework handles figures with complex annotations (e.g., spectral lines, redshift markers) common in astronomy.
Look for the evidence-indexed outline construction: does it require a pre-existing knowledge base or can it work with raw arXiv PDFs?
Examine the VLM-based visual analysis component: which VLM is used, and is it fine-tuned on scientific figures?

papers.title: It's not the Language Model, it's the Tool: Deterministic Mediation for Scientific Workflows
papers.authors: Marios Adamidis , Danae Katrisioti , Yannis Tzitzikas , Emmanuel Stratakis
papers.abstract: Language models can produce convincing scientific analyses, but repeated generations on the same data do not guarantee the same result. A researcher may regenerate an identical query and receive a different fit, a different peak position or a different analysis procedure, without an obvious way to decide which output to trust. We propose typed mediation, a pattern in which the model orchestrates deterministic tools rather than generating analytical code. Each tool encodes one researcher's exact procedure for one instrument, ported through structured interviews. The model selects which tool to call and with what parameters. The tool produces the result. Regeneration does not change it. We evaluate this claim by running the same photoluminescence analysis on four platforms, including three commercial foundation models, four times each with the same prompt. The typed tool produces identical results across all runs. The commercial platforms either vary in numerical output and analytical methodology across runs, or fail to produce valid results on the task. We deploy this pattern on two instruments serving users over approximately six months, with very positive user feedback. Both cases are very challenging: they involve proprietary binary formats and per-seat licensed software, which force the tool to remain on local infrastructure alongside the data and the instrument it operates. We argue that deployment topology is not just a preference, but a structural requirement of scientific tool mediation. The result is a practical pattern for deploying language models in scientific workflows where reproducibility is mandatory, reducing analysis time from weeks to minutes while guaranteeing identical outputs across runs.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses reproducibility in scientific workflows using LLMs, which is a key concern for automated scientific discovery and research agents in astronomy.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem that LLMs produce non-reproducible results when queried repeatedly on the same scientific data. The core idea is 'typed mediation': instead of having the LLM generate analytical code, it orchestrates deterministic, pre-built tools that encode exact researcher procedures, guaranteeing identical outputs across runs. For astronomy, this is highly relevant because reproducible analysis is critical for JWST and survey data, where one might want to automate SED fitting or spectral analysis without variability. A concrete workflow would be using an LLM agent to call a deterministic photometric redshift code or spectral fitting tool, ensuring identical results every time. A key caveat is that the tools must be pre-built and ported from researcher procedures, which requires upfront effort and domain expertise. Before investing time, check whether the paper provides a generic framework or only instrument-specific examples, and whether the typed mediation pattern can be adapted to astronomical tools like CIGALE or Prospector.

papers.title: Utility-Oriented Visual Evidence Selection for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Weiqing Luo , Zongye Hu , Xiao Wang , Zhiyuan Yu , Haofeng Zhang , Ziyi Huang
papers.subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: Visual evidence selection is a critical component of multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), yet existing methods typically rely on semantic relevance or surface-level similarity, which are often misaligned with the actual utility of visual evidence for downstream reasoning. We reformulate multimodal evidence selection from an information-theoretic perspective by defining evidence utility as the information gain induced on a model's output distribution. To overcome the intractability of answer-space optimization, we introduce a latent notion of evidence helpfulness and theoretically show that, under mild assumptions, ranking evidence by information gain on this latent variable is equivalent to answer-space utility. We further propose a training-free, surrogate-accelerated framework that efficiently estimates evidence utility using lightweight multimodal models. Experiments on MRAG-Bench and Visual-RAG across multiple model families demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art RAG baselines while achieving substantial reductions in computational cost.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses visual evidence selection for multimodal RAG, which is highly relevant to astronomical workflows combining images, spectra, and catalogs.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem that existing multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods select visual evidence based on semantic similarity, which may not be useful for downstream reasoning. The main idea is to reformulate evidence selection as maximizing information gain on the model's output distribution, using a training-free surrogate framework with lightweight multimodal models. For astronomy, this is highly relevant because it could enable RAG systems that retrieve the most useful JWST images, spectra, or catalog entries to answer scientific queries. A concrete workflow would be building a multimodal RAG system for a JWST survey where the model retrieves the most informative cutouts or spectra for a given question about a high-redshift galaxy. A key caveat is that the method is evaluated on general-domain benchmarks (MRAG-Bench, Visual-RAG), not on scientific or astronomical data. Before investing time, check whether the surrogate models used (lightweight multimodal models) can handle astronomical image formats (FITS, multi-band) and whether the framework can be adapted to domain-specific retrieval tasks.

papers.title: Mixed neural posterior estimation for simulators with discrete and continuous parameters
papers.authors: Jan Boelts , Cornelius Schröder , Jonas Beck , Jakob H. Macke , Michael Deistler , Daniel Gedon
papers.abstract: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) enables rapid parameter inference for complex simulators with intractable likelihoods. NPE trains an inference network to estimate a probability density over parameters given data, typically assumed to be \emph{continuous}. However, many scientific models involve parameter spaces that are \emph{mixed}, that is, they contain both discrete and continuous dimensions. We address this limitation by extending NPE to mixed parameter spaces through an inference network that jointly handles discrete and continuous parameters. The inference network factorizes the joint posterior into discrete and continuous components, combining an autoregressive classifier for the discrete parameters with a generative model for the continuous parameters, trained jointly under a single simulation-based objective. In addition, we propose a diagnostic tool to assess the calibration of the mixed posterior approximation. Across tractable toy examples and real-world scientific simulators, our joint inference approach yields accurate and calibrated posteriors. The inference framework is available in the \texttt{sbi} Python package.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper extends neural posterior estimation to mixed discrete/continuous parameter spaces, which is directly applicable to astronomical SED fitting and spectral fitting where parameters can be both continuous (e.g., redshift, metallicity) and discrete (e.g., galaxy type, AGN flag).
papers.Short digest: The paper addresses the limitation of neural posterior estimation (NPE) for simulators with mixed discrete and continuous parameters. The main idea is to use an inference network that factorizes the joint posterior into discrete and continuous components, combining an autoregressive classifier for discrete parameters with a generative model for continuous parameters. This matters for astronomy because many astronomical models (e.g., SED fitting, spectral fitting) have both discrete parameters (e.g., galaxy morphology class, AGN presence) and continuous parameters (e.g., redshift, stellar mass). I could imagine using this to perform Bayesian inference on JWST spectra of high-redshift galaxies, jointly estimating the probability of AGN vs. star-forming classification and continuous physical properties. A caveat is that the method requires a simulator that can generate mock data, which may be computationally expensive for complex astrophysical models.
Full-text inspection checklist: Look for the diagnostic tool to assess calibration of mixed posterior approximations.
Check the toy examples and real-world simulators used for validation.
See if the method is available in the sbi Python package and how to adapt it for custom simulators.
Examine the autoregressive classifier architecture for discrete parameters.

papers.title: VectorSmuggle: Steganographic Exfiltration in Embedding Stores and a Cryptographic Provenance Defense
papers.subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
papers.abstract: Modern retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems convert sensitive content into high-dimensional embeddings and store them in vector databases that treat the resulting numerical artifacts as opaque. Major vector-store products do not provide native controls for embedding integrity, ingestion-time distributional anomaly detection, or cryptographic provenance attestation. We show this opens a class of steganographic exfiltration attacks: an attacker with write access to the ingestion pipeline can hide payload data inside embeddings using simple post-embedding perturbations (noise injection, rotation, scaling, offset, fragmentation, and combinations thereof) while preserving the surface-level retrieval behavior the RAG system exposes to legitimate users. We evaluate these techniques across a synthetic-PII corpus on text-embedding-3-large, four locally hosted open embedding models, a cross-corpus replication on BEIR NFCorpus and a Quora subset (over 26,000 chunks combined), seven vector-store configurations, an adaptive-attacker variant of the detector evaluation, and a paraphrased-query retrieval benchmark. Distribution-shifting perturbations are often caught by simple anomaly detectors; small-angle orthogonal rotation defeats distribution-based detection across every (model, corpus) pair tested. A disjoint-Givens rotation encoder gives a closed-form per-vector capacity ceiling of floor(d/2) * b bits, but real embedding manifolds impose a capacity-detectability trade-off, and the retrieval-preserving operating point sits well below it. We propose VectorPin, a cryptographic provenance protocol that pins each embedding to its source content and producing model via an Ed25519 signature over a canonical byte representation. Any post-embedding modification breaks signature verification. Embedding-level integrity is a deployable, standardizable control that closes this attack class.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses security of RAG systems using vector databases, which is relevant for building reliable retrieval-augmented generation tools for astronomy literature and data.
papers.Short digest: This paper addresses the problem of steganographic attacks on vector databases used in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, where an attacker can hide payload data inside embeddings. The main idea is to show that simple perturbations like rotation can evade anomaly detection, and propose a cryptographic provenance protocol (VectorPin) to ensure embedding integrity. For astronomy, this is important if you build a RAG system to retrieve papers or data—you need to trust that the embeddings haven't been tampered with. A concrete workflow would be using VectorPin to verify that embeddings of astronomical catalogs or literature are authentic. A key caveat is that the paper focuses on security, not on improving retrieval quality, and the protocol adds overhead.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the VectorPin protocol is compatible with common vector database APIs (e.g., FAISS, Pinecone).
Look for benchmarks on retrieval performance degradation when using signed embeddings.
See if the paper discusses practical deployment for large-scale astronomical catalogs (e.g., millions of embeddings).
